title: Visakha's eight requests
hookLine: the great laywoman asks to give rain-cloths, food for travelers and medicine for the sick (Vinaya, Mahavagga 8)

cards: Rain over Savatthi. Visakha has invited the Buddha and the monks to a meal, and she sends a servant to the monastery to say it's time.
The servant comes back puzzled: there are no monks there, she reports, only naked ascetics standing out in the rain. Visakha understands right away.
Those are the monks, bathing in the rain, because they have no cloths to bathe in. She sends the servant back. And while the meal is being served, an idea is forming.
Afterward, she asks the Buddha for something, for as long as she lives.

teach.b: First, the asking. In the account in the Vinaya, the monastic rule, she asks the Buddha for eight boons. The awakened, he says, have gone beyond granting boons.
These are proper and blameless, she answers. Then speak, he says. Second, the list, and how down-to-earth it is.

Cloths for the monks to bathe in during the rains. Food for monks arriving in town, who don't yet know where to go for alms. Food for monks setting out on a journey, so they don't fall behind their companions.
Food for the sick, so they don't get worse. Food for those who nurse the sick, so they don't have to choose between their own meal and their patient. Medicine for the sick.
Rice gruel, given regularly. And bathing cloths for the nuns, who, she had heard, were being mocked as they bathed in the river. Each one fills a gap she noticed.
Third, the Buddha's question. What benefit do you see in this, Visakha?
When she hears that a monk who has died once used her rain-cloth, or ate her food, or took her medicine, she says, she'll be glad.
From gladness, joy; from joy, calm; from calm, ease; and her mind will settle.
That, she says, will develop her own practice. Fourth, the result. The Buddha praises her and grants all eight.
It's generosity that pays attention: who's arriving, who's leaving, who's sick, and who's quietly worn out from caring for the sick.

how: In Theravada communities, lay Buddhists give monasteries robes, food and medicine, and Visakha's requests are read in the Vinaya as the story behind the monks' rain-bathing cloth.

o: a boon or wish asked for

games.q: the eight requests: tap the pairs.
p: leading to calm and a settled mind

s: Visakha asked the Buddha for eight things for herself
every request was for the monks and nuns.
her servant mistook the bathing monks for naked ascetics
they had no cloths to bathe in, which gave Visakha the idea.
the Buddha refused, since the awakened don't grant boons
he said they had gone beyond boons, but when she said hers were blameless, he heard her and granted all eight.

games.q: you're Visakha. your servant says there are no monks at the monastery, only naked ascetics bathing in the rain. what do you do?
o: assume the monks have left town.
realize the monks have no rain-cloths, and plan to give some.
games.why: she understands they're the monks, with no cloths to bathe in, and rain-cloths become the first of her eight requests.

practice: Go through the people near you this week the way Visakha went through what the monks and nuns lacked: who's arriving somewhere new, who's leaving, who's sick, who's caring for someone sick and forgetting to eat.
Let one person come forward, and picture one plain, useful thing that would meet their need. Not grand; exact.

wordCard.voice: Vara, a boon or wish. What Visakha asked the Buddha for eight of: rain-cloths, food for travelers, the sick and their nurses, and medicine. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali vara, a boon or wish: Visakha asks the Buddha for eight.

carryVoice: Your line: practical kindness. Generosity can start with simply noticing. Day seven hundred sixty-four, done.
